{{Short description|Theorem}}
In mathematics, especially in [[differential topology]], '''Thom's first isotopy lemma''' states: given a smooth map <math>f : M \to N</math> between smooth manifolds and <math>S \subset M</math> a closed [[Whitney conditions|Whitney stratified subset]], if <math>f|_S</math> is proper and <math>f|_A</math> is a submersion for each stratum <math>A</math> of <math>S</math>, then <math>f|_S</math> is a locally trivial [[fibration]].<ref name=Mather>{{harvnb|Mather|2012|loc=Proposition 11.1.}}</ref> The lemma was originally introduced by [[René Thom]] who considered the case when <math>N = \mathbb{R}</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Thom|1969}}</ref> In that case, the lemma constructs an [[Homotopy#Isotopy|isotopy]] from the fiber <math>f^{-1}(a)</math> to <math>f^{-1}(b)</math>; whence the name "isotopy lemma".

The local trivializations that the lemma provide preserve the strata. However, they are generally not smooth (not even <math>C^1</math>). On the other hand, it is possible that local trivializations are semialgebraic if the input data is semialgebraic.<ref>https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=t8n5yFLUPuIC&pg=PA83&lpg=PA83#v=onepage&q&f=false in {{cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=t8n5yFLUPuIC&pg=PA83 | title=Real Analytic and Algebraic Geometry: Proceedings of the International Conference, Trento (Italy), September 21-25th, 1992 | isbn=9783110881271 | last1=Broglia | first1=Fabrizio | last2=Galbiati | first2=Margherita | last3=Tognoli | first3=Alberto | date=11 July 2011 | publisher=Walter de Gruyter }}</ref><ref>Editorial note: in fact, local trivializations can be definable if the input date is definable, according to https://ncatlab.org/toddtrimble/published/Surface+diagrams</ref>

The lemma is also valid for a more general stratified space such as a [[Mather stratified space|stratified space in the sense of Mather]] but still with the Whitney conditions (or some other conditions). The lemma is also valid for the stratification that satisfies [[Bekka's condition (C)]], which is weaker than Whitney's condition (B).<ref>§ 3 of {{cite book |last1=Bekka |first1=K. |title=Singularity Theory and its Applications |chapter=C-Régularité et trivialité topologique |series=Lecture Notes in Mathematics |date=1991 |volume=1462 |pages=42–62 |doi=10.1007/BFb0086373 |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/BFb0086373 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-540-53737-3 |language=en}}</ref> (The significance of this is that the consequences of the first isotopy lemma cannot imply Whitney’s condition (B).)

[[Thom's second isotopy lemma]] is a family version of the first isotopy lemma.

==Proof==

The proof<ref name=Mather /> is based on the notion of a '''controlled vector field'''.<ref>{{harvnb|Mather|2012|loc=$ 9.}}</ref> Let <math>\{ (T_A, \pi_A, \rho_A) \mid A \}</math> be a system of [[tubular neighborhood]]s <math>T_A</math> in <math>M</math> of strata <math>A</math> in <math>S</math> where <math>\pi_A : T_A \to A</math> is the associated projection and <math>\rho_A : T_A \to [0, \infty)</math> given by the square norm on each fiber of <math>\pi_A</math>. (The construction of such a system relies on the Whitney conditions or something weaker.) By definition, a controlled [[vector field]] is a family of vector fields (smooth of some class) <math>\eta_A</math> on the strata <math>A</math> such that: for each stratum ''A'', there exists a neighborhood <math>T'_A</math> of <math>A</math> in <math>T_A</math> such that for any <math>B > A</math>,
:<math>\eta_B \circ \rho_A = 0,</math>
:<math>(\pi_A)_* \eta_B = \eta_A \circ \pi_A</math>
on <math>T_A' \cap B</math>.

Assume the system <math>T_A</math> is compatible with the map <math>f : M \to N</math> (such a system exists). Then there are two key results due to Thom:
# Given a vector field <math>\zeta</math> on ''N'', there exists a controlled vector field <math>\eta</math> on ''S'' that is a lift of it: <math>f_* (\eta) = \zeta \circ f</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Mather|2012|loc=Proposition 9.1.}}</ref>
# A controlled vector field has a ''continuous'' flow (despite the fact that a controlled vector field is discontinuous).<ref>{{harvnb|Mather|2012|loc=Proposition 10.1.}}</ref>

The lemma now follows in a straightforward fashion. Since the statement is local, assume <math>N = \mathbb{R}^n</math> and <math>\partial_i</math> the coordinate vector fields on <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>. Then, by the lifting result, we find controlled vector fields <math>\widetilde{\partial_i}</math> on <math>S</math> such that <math>f_*(\widetilde{\partial_i}) = \partial_i \circ f</math>. Let <math>\varphi_i : \mathbb{R} \times S \to S</math> be the flows associated to them. Then define
:<math>H : f|_S^{-1}(0) \times \mathbb{R}^n \to S</math>
by
:<math>H(y, t) = \varphi_n(t_n, \phi_{n-1}(t_{n-1}, \cdots, \varphi_1(t_1, y) \cdots)).</math>
It is a map over <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> and is a [[homeomorphism]] since <math>G(x) = (\varphi_1(-t_1, \cdots, \varphi_n(-t_n, x) \cdots), t), t = f(x)</math> is the inverse. Since the flows <math>\varphi_i</math> preserve the strata, <math>H</math> also preserves the strata. <math>\square</math>
